children: GSMA says India’s 60 million SMEs could drive the next phase of enterprise 5G adoption as operators seek greater value from deployed networks

India's next phase of 5G growth will depend on enterprises, particularly the country's 60 million small and medium enterprises (SMEs), as operators look to generate greater value from networks that have already been deployed, Jeanette Whyte, Head of Public Policy and External Affairs, Asia Pacific at GSMA, told BW Businessworld in an interview on the sidelines of India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi.
“Now we've rolled it out, we need to get value out of it, and I think that's where we'll see a lot of growth in the enterprises,” Whyte said.

India has around 1.2 billion active mobile connections and almost 450 million 5G connections, according to a GSMA report seen by BW Businessworld. The report identifies AI-ready networks, enterprise digitisation and digital trust as key priorities for India as it looks to translate its connectivity scale into greater economic value.

India has around 450 million 5G subscribers, but most of the current adoption is among consumers, Whyte said. While enterprise use cases were a major part of the promise around 5G, adoption has not yet matched expectations globally.
“The promise of 5G was very much on the side of enterprise, and perhaps it's not quite lived up to what we expected. Not just in India, that's everywhere,” she said.
SMEs Seen As Next Opportunity

Whyte sees India's 60 million SMEs as a major opportunity for operators as businesses begin to use 5G for more than connectivity. She said enterprise adoption would take time and investment, with manufacturing among the sectors where 5G could have a stronger role.

“I would also say, well look, about the SMEs, they are [the country's] lifeblood, and I think if they start using it then you can offer new services, security, AI services that you could add on top,” she said.

The GSMA report also points to private networks, fixed wireless access, cloud connectivity, network APIs and cybersecurity services as areas that can help businesses adopt digital technologies and create new growth opportunities.

Whyte said the transition would not mean that every enterprise would need 5G. Manufacturing, in particular, could be better suited to applications such as remote operations, while enterprises and operators would need to work together to identify viable use cases.
Operators Need More Monetisation

For telecom operators, the next phase will also require greater monetisation of networks. Whyte said operators could layer services such as security and AI on top of connectivity as enterprise adoption expands.

The GSMA continues to oppose setting aside separate portions of mobile spectrum specifically for enterprises, arguing that spectrum allocated to mobile operators can be used more efficiently. Whyte pointed to Germany as an example where uptake of dedicated enterprise spectrum had not been strong.

India's existing framework allows spectrum sharing and provides enterprises with avenues to access spectrum, she said, making greater collaboration between operators and businesses possible without carving out separate spectrum pools.
Trust Becomes Critical
As connectivity moves into more business and financial applications, Whyte said trust would become important.

The GSMA report found that 12 per cent of respondents in India had been scammed in the previous year, while 72 per cent said the growing risk of scams had changed their behaviour. Among reported cases, 33 per cent remained unresolved, while 67 per cent of victims who lost money recovered none of it.

The report said faster case resolution, better recovery and closer coordination between public authorities, banks, mobile operators and digital platforms would be needed to strengthen consumer protection and digital trust.

Whyte said network-level intelligence could provide an additional layer of protection. Operators can use network APIs to identify signals such as a recent SIM change, which can then be used by banks or digital platforms when assessing potentially suspicious activity.

The report said Indian operators, including Airtel, Reliance Jio and Vodafone Idea, support GSMA Open Gateway, which provides common technical frameworks for capabilities such as number verification and SIM swap signals.

She also stressed that mobile networks alone cannot address the problem, as scams frequently take place on digital platforms. Cross-sector and cross border cooperation between operators, financial institutions, platforms and governments will therefore be necessary.
India Eyes 6G Leadership

Beyond the current 5G rollout, the GSMA sees an opportunity for India to play a larger role in 6G development. Whyte said India had taken a number of steps towards becoming a 6G leader, but would need to remain aligned with global standards and interoperability if it wants to turn its technology capabilities into export opportunities.

The GSMA report also said India has an opportunity to play a leading role in 6G development. Mobile operators and industry partners across Asia Pacific, including the Bharat 6G Alliance, have signed the GSMA's Tokyo Accord, which calls for open, interoperable and trusted digital ecosystems for the 6G era.
Whyte said the focus for India should ultimately be on building a digital economy that can translate connectivity and innovation into commercial outcomes.
